title: Grouping numbers into ranges with pd.cut

cells.text: Back to the players. Managers often want **categories** instead of raw numbers, like Casual, Regular and Hardcore players. You could write a function with if/elif, but pandas has a shortcut: `pd.cut()`. It's the pandas version of CASE WHEN in SQL.

cells.prompt: Press Run to load the players table.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("players.csv")
df.head()

cells.text: `pd.cut()` sorts numbers into ranges called **bins**. `bins=[0, 100, 300, 1000]` gives the edges, which make 3 ranges: over 0 up to 100, over 100 up to 300, and over 300 up to 1000. Each range **includes its top number**, so exactly 100 hours counts as the first range. `labels` names the ranges, in order.

cells.prompt: Press Run to label every player.
How many players are Regular (over 100, up to 300 hours)? Look at the table above, then pick one and press Run.

cells.text: value_counts() sorts by count, so the levels came out in a mixed order. Add `.sort_index()` to put them back in label order: Casual, Regular, Hardcore.

cells.prompt: Your turn: count the players in each level, in the order Casual, Regular, Hardcore.
hints: Add .sort_index() to the end of the cell above.

cells.prompt: Replace ___ so that Regular means over 100 and up to 500 hours, then press Run to see the new counts.
hints: The bins list holds the edges between ranges, in order.

cells.text: The new level column works with everything you know, including groupby. When you group by a column made with pd.cut, add `observed=True` inside groupby(). It keeps only the levels that actually appear and avoids a warning.

cells.prompt: Last one: show the average hours per level, rounded to 1 decimal. Use the level column from earlier.
hints: df.groupby("level", observed=True), pick hours_played, mean, round(1).

recap: pd.cut(column, bins=[...], labels=[...]) turns numbers into categories. Each range includes its top number. Use sort_index() for label order and observed=True when grouping.
